newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore sees big gains in WTO.
newsitem.headline: Singapore sees big gains in WTO.

text.p: Singapore's winning campaign to host the first World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting reflects its ambition to play a key role in shaping global free trade, the lifeblood of its economy, analysts said.
"As one of the world's most externally oriented economies, Singapore has a disproportionately large stake in the WTO," said Desmond Supple, economist at independent research house I.D.E.A.
"Singapore stands to benefit more than most from continued global trade liberalisation as trade is the engine of its growth...," he said.
The city-state met U.S. opposition two years ago in its bid to host the meeting, which is expected to draw 4,000 officials from 160 countries December 9-13.
U.S. DISPLEASURE

In a stance some analysts said had reflected U.S. displeasure with Singapore's caning of an American teenager for vandalism, U.S. Trade Representative Mickey Kantor had said the meeting ought to be held at WTO headquarters in Geneva.
But Singapore won, thanks to support from other WTO members.

Derek da Cunha, senior fellow at the government-linked Institute of South East Asian Studies (ISEAS), said Singapore's hosting of the conference "carries a great deal of symbolism for the city-state, underscoring its commitment to free trade and its trading links across the globe."

Besides the international prestige Singapore would gain, "there is a genuine national interest in fostering better global free trade and an open market," said Tan Kong Yam, head of Business Policy at the National University of Singapore.
In June, the WTO hailed Singapore for its open-market policies but the European Union and other trading powers called on Singapore to speed up liberalisation of its services sector.

At the ministerial meeting, trade ministers will review the work of the WTO and the implementation of free-trade commitments made under the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT).
However, Supple said the struggle that Singapore endured to land the gathering would be repeated during the meeting itself.
"There is tension every step of the way," he said, referring to differences between the West and developing countries over the issue of linking trade liberalisation with labour rights.
He added that the prestige Singapore may gain by having the world spotlight focused on its record as one of the world's most open economies would not automatically result in any real benefits.
"This is quite intangible as the prestige factor may not necessarily lead to any additional investment and trade flows to this region," he said.
GOOD FOR TOURISM
However, Tan said the large numbers of people coming to Singapore for the meeting would benefit the local tourism industry.

Although a slice of Singapore's workforce would be mobilised to ensure the meeting comes off without a hitch, Tan said, the average Singaporean would probabaly not be too concerned about some of the trade issues involved.
"But the more educated public will realise that these things are important for Singapore as a small economy."

Supple said any political gains the Singapore government would reap from the meeting, ahead of a general election due by April 1997, would stem from how successful it was in pushing its economic agenda.

"If there are any movements toward freer trade, then Singapore's economy and the electorate would gain," he said. "But I don't think it would be wise to play up the political aspect of this. I think political issues will take secondary importance to all these economic issues that will be displayed."
